parsed_answer.content: Wildcards in Java generics, denoted by the question mark (?), are a mechanism to provide flexibility in type parameterization, allowing for covariance and contravariance that standard invariant generic types cannot express. In Java, List<String> is not a subtype of List<Object>, a design choice that prevents heap pollution and ensures type safety at runtime. Wildcards solve the 'inflexibility' problem by allowing methods to accept a broader range of types while maintaining compile-time checks. The 'extends' keyword (upper-bounded wildcard) enables covariance, meaning you can read from a structure containing any subtype of a specified class. Conversely, the 'super' keyword (lower-bounded wildcard) enables contravariance, allowing you to write to a structure by defining a base type that is a superclass of the intended object, ensuring that the collection can safely hold the provided type.

rows: Producer Extends (PECS): Reading data from a collection safely.
Consumer Super (PECS): Writing data into a collection safely.
When only Object-level methods are needed (e.g., size()).

items: The PECS principle (Producer Extends, Consumer Super) is the golden rule: if you are retrieving items from a collection, use '? extends T'; if you are adding items to a collection, use '? super T'.
Upper-bounded wildcards (? extends T) make a collection effectively immutable for writes, because the compiler cannot guarantee the specific type being inserted, only that it is a subtype of T.
Lower-bounded wildcards (? super T) allow you to add objects of type T or its subtypes, but reading from such a collection returns only Object, as the exact lower bound is unknown.
Wildcards are erased at runtime due to Type Erasure, meaning the JVM sees only the upper bound (or Object if unbounded), making reflection-based type inspection limited.

parsed_answer.content: A common trap for developers is attempting to use wildcards in class definitions (e.g., class Box<? extends T> {}). Wildcards are intended for use in method signatures, field declarations, and local variables to define API contracts, not for defining the generic type parameters of a class itself. If you find yourself needing a wildcard in a class definition, you likely need a type parameter (T) instead.
